passages.title: Job loses his children and wealth
passages.summary: Satan questions Job’s reasons for serving God. Four messengers report losses. Job mourns and worships.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me reads the heavenly exchange as poetry about an accuser’s challenge.

contextNote.title: The reader knows what the friends do not
contextNote.text: The opening calls Job blameless before his suffering begins. His friends later reason from suffering back to guilt. Their conclusion conflicts with information the reader already has. That difference shapes the long debate. Read confident advice against the book’s opening, not only the speaker’s certainty.

passages.title: Illness and silent friends
passages.summary: Job suffers painful sores. His wife urges him to renounce God. Three friends sit silently with him.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks why faith should continue when expected rewards disappear.

contextNote.title: Silence comes before the argument
contextNote.text: The friends first share Job’s ground and silence. Their presence recognizes pain before their speeches try to explain it. Compare this quiet company with the accusations that follow.

passages.title: Job wishes he had not been born
passages.summary: Job curses the day of his birth. He asks why people in pain must keep living.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me allows questions and faith to remain together during suffering.

contextNote.title: Grief reverses the language of birth
contextNote.text: Job wishes his birth could disappear from time. Darkness replaces the light normally linked with new life. His speech attacks the beginning of his existence, rather than describing a cure.

passages.title: Eliphaz explains suffering through guilt
passages.summary: Eliphaz recalls Job’s help for others. He claims innocent people do not perish.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine the friends’ claim that pain proves guilt.

contextNote.title: Past counsel becomes a charge
contextNote.text: Eliphaz recalls Job strengthening other people. He then treats Job’s own distress as failure to follow that advice. The change turns remembered kindness into pressure on its giver.

passages.title: Eliphaz urges Job to accept correction
passages.summary: Eliphaz urges Job to seek God. He promises safety, children, and long life after correction.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions the friends’ explanation that God is punishing Job.

contextNote.title: Advice assumes an explanation
contextNote.text: Eliphaz calls suffering a form of divine correction. That explanation makes acceptance seem the proper response. Readers already know the opening did not identify Job’s loss as punishment.

passages.title: Job asks his friends for kindness
passages.summary: Job describes pain beyond his strength. He compares his friends to streams that disappear when needed.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job asks for kindness before a verdict. How could his friends answer that request?

contextNote.title: Failed friendship becomes a dry stream
contextNote.text: Job compares his friends with water that disappears when travelers need it. The image concerns disappointed dependence, not merely harsh speech. Their promised help fails precisely when his need grows greatest.

passages.title: Job addresses God in his pain
passages.summary: Job describes sleepless nights and painful skin. He asks God to leave him alone.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job speaks directly to God about pain. What does he ask God to change?

contextNote.title: Attention can feel like pursuit
contextNote.text: Job asks why God watches people so closely. Divine attention here feels burdensome rather than comforting. His appeal for rest challenges an easy equation between being seen and feeling safe.

passages.title: Bildad blames wrongdoing
passages.summary: Bildad suggests Job’s children died for their sins. He promises renewed success if Job is upright.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what goes wrong when friends explain pain through blame.

contextNote.title: An argument makes the dead guilty
contextNote.text: Bildad explains the children’s deaths through their supposed sin. His tidy account gives Job another wound. Distinguish Bildad’s confidence from the book’s opening description of the household.

passages.title: Job asks who could judge his case
passages.summary: Job describes God’s power over mountains, stars, and seas. He seeks someone to hear both sides.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job wants someone to hear both sides. What prevents him from feeling heard?

contextNote.title: A court requires more than an argument
contextNote.text: Job pictures a dispute without an impartial judge between its parties. God’s power makes a fair hearing seem impossible. Legal language exposes his need for access, not simply a better defense.

passages.title: Job asks why his maker harms him
passages.summary: Job recalls how God formed his body and gave him life. He asks why God now opposes him.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job recalls the care that formed him. Why does his present pain make that memory difficult?

contextNote.title: Creation becomes grounds for complaint
contextNote.text: Job recalls God carefully forming his body. He asks why its maker now seems to destroy it. The creation image gives his protest a personal claim on divine care.

passages.title: Zophar demands that Job change
passages.summary: Zophar says Job deserves worse. He promises relief if Job removes wrongdoing from his home.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions Zophar’s claim that Job’s pain comes from wrongdoing.

contextNote.title: Certainty closes the hearing
contextNote.text: Zophar claims Job deserves worse than his present suffering. His appeal to hidden wisdom prevents Job from challenging that claim. A speech about knowledge therefore ends by refusing to hear the sufferer.

passages.title: Job challenges his friends’ wisdom
passages.summary: Job says he understands as much as his friends. He points to robbers who live safely.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what Job knows about God while challenging his friends.

contextNote.title: Creation does not settle the dispute
contextNote.text: Job also knows the language of animals and divine power. That shared knowledge does not make his friends’ explanation true. He describes overturned rulers to question a simple connection between status and righteousness.

passages.title: Job seeks a hearing with God
passages.summary: Job accuses his friends of speaking falsely for God. He asks God to hear his case.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me follows the King James Bible’s reading about trusting God. How does that reading differ from the World English Bible here?

contextNote.title: Defending God can involve false speech
contextNote.text: Job calls his friends poor healers and challenges their defense of God. He wants to speak directly rather than accept their account. The scene asks whether religious loyalty excuses misleading claims about another person.

passages.title: Job asks whether the dead live again
passages.summary: Job compares short human life with a tree that can grow again. He asks God to remember him.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects this question with resurrection through Jesus Christ. What does Job ask God to remember?

contextNote.title: A tree offers hope people lack
contextNote.text: A cut tree can send out new shoots. Job places that return beside human death and disappearance. His later wish for renewed life remains a question within this contrast.

passages.title: Eliphaz condemns Job’s words
passages.summary: Eliphaz says Job’s own words prove guilt. He describes the fear and loss awaiting wicked people.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Eliphaz treats protest as proof of guilt. What happens when listeners make that assumption?

contextNote.title: A friend treats protest as danger
contextNote.text: Eliphaz now charges Job with undermining reverence itself. The dispute moves from Job’s circumstances to his right to speak. His account of wicked lives becomes accusation disguised as general instruction.

passages.title: Job calls his friends poor comforters
passages.summary: Job says he would strengthen them if their places were reversed. He asks for a witness in heaven.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how friends can strengthen someone instead of adding blame.

contextNote.title: A witness is needed beyond the friends
contextNote.text: Job names his friends as failed comforters before seeking a witness above. Human listeners have not made his suffering understandable. His hope for testimony grows from the collapse of the present conversation.

passages.title: Job sees his hope nearing the grave
passages.summary: Job describes broken plans and public shame. He asks where his hope can go.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job’s plans have broken apart. What kind of help could reach him now?

contextNote.title: False brightness cannot remove death
contextNote.text: Job describes others calling darkness light while the grave approaches. Their assurances do not match the body before them. His questions about hope force readers to face that mismatch.

passages.title: Bildad describes the wicked person’s ruin
passages.summary: Bildad describes traps, disease, lost children, and a forgotten name. He calls this the wicked person’s fate.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Bildad describes the loss of a name and children. How might Job hear those words?

contextNote.title: A general picture targets one sufferer
contextNote.text: Bildad describes traps, lost descendants, and destroyed homes. These images closely resemble Job’s losses without naming him. A speech presented as general wisdom therefore presses a personal accusation.

passages.title: Job asks for pity and a defender
passages.summary: Job describes relatives, servants, and friends turning away. He declares that his Redeemer lives.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me reads Job’s Redeemer as Jesus Christ. A redeemer saves or defends someone. What help does Job hope for?

contextNote.title: An appeal interrupts accusation
contextNote.text: Job asks the friends for pity before speaking of a defender. His damaged relationships make recognition as urgent as explanation. Read the hope for vindication beside his immediate request to stop the attack.

passages.title: Zophar says wicked success ends quickly
passages.summary: Zophar describes stolen wealth turning into suffering. He says wicked people cannot keep their success.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Zophar links wickedness with brief success. What evidence would challenge his claim?

contextNote.title: Zophar pictures wealth as swallowed food
contextNote.text: The wicked person consumes riches and must give them back. This bodily image makes injustice seem certain to punish its owner. Job’s next speech challenges whether actual lives always follow that pattern.

passages.title: Job points to wicked people who prosper
passages.summary: Job describes wicked people growing old with safe homes and thriving children. He challenges his friends’ answers.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the contrast between wicked success and faithful suffering.

contextNote.title: Observation challenges the friends’ rule
contextNote.text: Job points to wicked people who live long and prosper. Their children and homes survive while his own did not. These examples test the friends’ explanation against events rather than merely another theory.

passages.title: Eliphaz names sins he assumes Job committed
passages.summary: Eliphaz accuses Job of withholding food, clothing, and help. He urges Job to return to God.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Eliphaz’s accusation to ask how friends can offer better help.

contextNote.title: Suspicion becomes an invented charge
contextNote.text: Eliphaz now names specific offenses against poor people. The speech treats its explanation of suffering as evidence of those offenses. Compare these charges with Job’s later account of his public conduct.

passages.title: Job searches for God’s court
passages.summary: Job wants to present his case to God. He cannot find him, but insists he kept his commands.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Job’s search with faith during unanswered questions.

contextNote.title: Absence prevents a hearing
contextNote.text: Job imagines presenting his case before God. He searches in every direction but cannot find that court. His confidence in his conduct exists beside fear of a power he cannot approach.

passages.title: Job describes the suffering of the poor
passages.summary: Job describes stolen fields, hungry workers, and people without shelter. He asks why justice seems delayed.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses other Church scripture to study suffering. Which examples show Job’s concern for people beyond himself?

contextNote.title: A complaint extends beyond one household
contextNote.text: Job describes workers, hungry families, and people driven from shelter. Their injuries remain visible without swift public judgment. His protest now asks why a whole pattern of harm goes unanswered.

passages.title: Bildad questions human purity
passages.summary: Bildad says God rules above and even the stars lack purity before him. He compares people to worms.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Bildad speaks about human weakness. Does his answer address what Job asked?

contextNote.title: A short speech leaves the case unheard
contextNote.text: Bildad answers with human smallness before God. This claim does not address the injured people Job just described. The shrinking response shows how general claims can avoid a concrete dispute.

passages.title: Job describes power beyond human knowledge
passages.summary: Job first asks how Bildad has helped him. He describes God’s power over sky, sea, and death.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job asks how Bildad helped him. What separates an impressive speech from useful comfort?

contextNote.title: Shared beliefs do not guarantee useful help
contextNote.text: Job asks whom Bildad’s speech has strengthened. He then describes divine power in language equally grand. The contrast separates impressive claims about God from help that meets a sufferer’s need.

passages.title: Job holds to his innocence
passages.summary: Job refuses to admit the friends are right about him. He then describes the fate of oppressors.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job refuses a false confession. Why would admitting his friends are right matter?

contextNote.title: Job refuses a purchased agreement
contextNote.text: Job will not confess guilt simply to end the dispute. His hold on integrity stands beside descriptions of wicked people’s ruin. Agreement about some judgments does not require accepting the friends’ charge against him.

passages.title: Where can wisdom be found?
passages.summary: A poem describes miners finding hidden metals. It asks where wisdom lies and says God knows its way.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The poem separates treasure from wisdom. What can skill and wealth fail to teach?

contextNote.title: Mining skill exposes another limit
contextNote.text: People can reach hidden metals beneath the earth. Yet the poem asks where wisdom can be found. The contrast separates technical success from understanding how life should be lived.

passages.title: Job remembers respect and service
passages.summary: Job recalls public honor and his children nearby. He remembers helping widows and people in need.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job remembers helping people in need. How does that memory answer Eliphaz’s accusations?

contextNote.title: Memory defines the lost public role
contextNote.text: Job remembers helping people who lacked defenders. His former honor rests on these acts as well as wealth. Read this account against Eliphaz’s accusations about how he treated the poor.

passages.title: Job describes shame and unanswered cries
passages.summary: Job contrasts former respect with mockery and pain. He says his calls to God receive no answer.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job’s neighbors add mockery to pain. What could they change without knowing why he suffers?

contextNote.title: The remembered world has been reversed
contextNote.text: Job’s former respect becomes ridicule and isolation. His appeal to God receives no answer within the speech. The final change from music to mourning gives this reversal a sound.

passages.title: Job gives his final defense
passages.summary: Job lists wrongs he says he avoided. He describes fairness toward servants, generosity, and welcome for strangers.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me recalls Job’s repeated request for God to answer him.

contextNote.title: A measure becomes an image of justice
contextNote.text: Job asks for a fair weighing of his life. He then names concrete duties toward workers, poor people, and strangers. His claim concerns conduct, not only private feelings. The image of weighing makes impartial judgment visible. An ancient trade weight helps explain the image without identifying Job’s time or home.

passages.title: Elihu begins after the others fall silent
passages.summary: Elihu becomes angry with Job and his three friends. He says youth does not prevent understanding.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu waited for older speakers. Does his anger help him listen?

contextNote.title: Age does not settle authority
contextNote.text: Elihu explains why he waited before speaking. He then claims understanding does not belong to age alone. His entrance changes the speakers without yet providing readers an independent verdict on his claims.

passages.title: Elihu says suffering can teach
passages.summary: Elihu says God speaks through dreams and pain. He describes rescue through a messenger and renewed health.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu says pain can teach. How could that idea help or hurt someone in distress?

contextNote.title: An equal listener claims to explain God
contextNote.text: Elihu first stresses his shared human condition with Job. He then interprets dreams and pain as divine instruction. The move from equal listener to teacher helps explain the pressure within his appeal.

passages.title: Elihu defends God’s justice
passages.summary: Elihu says God treats rich and poor without favor. He accuses Job of adding rebellion to sin.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu defends fairness while accusing Job. What evidence supports his charge?

contextNote.title: A principle takes the place of a hearing
contextNote.text: Elihu insists God cannot act wrongly. He uses that conviction to condemn Job’s words. The argument defends divine justice without answering the particular losses that produced Job’s protest.

passages.title: Elihu challenges Job’s complaint
passages.summary: Elihu says human choices affect other people. He claims pride prevents cries for help from being heard.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu links unanswered cries with pride. What would Job’s earlier words challenge?

contextNote.title: Unheard cries receive another explanation
contextNote.text: Elihu links unanswered cries with pride and inadequate understanding. That claim shifts attention from oppression toward the petitioner. Read his explanation as Elihu’s judgment, not the book’s independent finding.

passages.title: Elihu describes correction and the storm
passages.summary: Elihu says suffering opens people’s ears to instruction. He describes rain, clouds, and lightning.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu promises good years after obedience. How does that promise compare with Job’s experience?

contextNote.title: Instruction and threat share one speech
contextNote.text: Elihu presents affliction as a means of opening ears. He also warns Job against choices that could worsen his condition. The speech combines an offer of meaning with pressure to accept it.

passages.title: Elihu asks Job to consider God’s works
passages.summary: Elihu describes thunder, snow, and changing weather. He asks whether Job understands their workings.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu asks about weather beyond human control. What changes when the next speaker is the Lord?

contextNote.title: Weather prepares a change of voice
contextNote.text: Elihu asks Job to consider wonders beyond his control. Thunder and cloud imagery widen the scene beyond the dispute. The following divine speech comes from a whirlwind, continuing that change of scale.

passages.title: The Lord answers from the whirlwind
passages.summary: The Lord questions Job about earth, sea, dawn, weather, stars, and animals.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects the joyful sons of God with life before birth. What does God ask Job about creation?

contextNote.title: Questions change the scale of the debate
contextNote.text: God’s questions begin with a world older than Job. They do not reveal the opening conversation that readers know. The reply changes the field of attention without giving a direct cause for the losses.

passages.title: The Lord describes wild animals
passages.summary: The Lord asks about goats, wild donkeys, oxen, ostriches, horses, hawks, and eagles.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how the creatures in God’s speech change the reader’s view.

contextNote.title: Wild creatures live beyond human service
contextNote.text: The animals described here need not obey or benefit people. Their freedom and unusual habits matter within the speech. The world’s value therefore exceeds its usefulness to the person asking for an explanation.

passages.title: Job falls silent and hears about behemoth
passages.summary: Job places his hand over his mouth. The Lord questions his judgment and describes behemoth’s strength.
passages.uncertainty: The poem names the Jordan. This marker does not locate Job’s home.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to consider God’s creations from different views.

contextNote.title: Judgment includes the power to govern
contextNote.text: God connects Job’s challenge with the ability to bring proud people low. The questions test more than skill in making an argument. The powerful creature that follows adds another limit to human control.

passages.title: The Lord describes Leviathan
passages.summary: The Lord describes Leviathan’s scales, strength, and frightening breath. Human tools cannot subdue it.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The poem describes Leviathan beyond human control. What does that show about the limits of power?

contextNote.title: A creature resists the language of ownership
contextNote.text: Questions about catching Leviathan turn into an account of its strength. The creature cannot become an ordinary servant or household possession. Its resistance makes human claims to command the wider world seem small.

passages.title: Job answers and prays for his friends
passages.summary: Job answers the Lord. The Lord rebukes the three friends. Job prays for them and receives renewed prosperity.
passages.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects Job’s renewed life with hope after loss. What must the friends do after God corrects them?

contextNote.title: The final judgment changes how the speeches should be read
contextNote.text: God rejects the friends’ speech even though they defended divine justice. Job’s prayer for them then becomes part of the ending. Restoration does not supply a simple explanation for the earlier deaths. The book leaves a difference between renewed life and answered questions. Its final judgment warns against using certainty to explain another person’s pain.

events.title: Job loses his children and wealth
events.summary: Satan questions Job’s reasons for serving God. Four messengers report losses. Job mourns and worships.
events.detail: The opening calls Job blameless before his suffering begins. His friends later reason from suffering back to guilt. Their conclusion conflicts with information the reader already has. events.title: Illness and silent friends
events.summary: Job suffers painful sores. His wife urges him to renounce God. Three friends sit silently with him.
events.detail: The friends first share Job’s ground and silence. Their presence recognizes pain before their speeches try to explain it. Compare this quiet company with the accusations that follow.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks why faith should continue when expected rewards disappear.

events.title: Job wishes he had not been born
events.summary: Job curses the day of his birth. He asks why people in pain must keep living.
events.detail: Job wishes his birth could disappear from time. Darkness replaces the light normally linked with new life. His speech attacks the beginning of his existence, rather than describing a cure.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me allows questions and faith to remain together during suffering.

events.title: Eliphaz explains suffering through guilt
events.summary: Eliphaz recalls Job’s help for others. He claims innocent people do not perish.
events.detail: Eliphaz recalls Job strengthening other people. He then treats Job’s own distress as failure to follow that advice. The change turns remembered kindness into pressure on its giver.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine the friends’ claim that pain proves guilt.

events.title: Eliphaz urges Job to accept correction
events.summary: Eliphaz urges Job to seek God. He promises safety, children, and long life after correction.
events.detail: Eliphaz calls suffering a form of divine correction. That explanation makes acceptance seem the proper response. Readers already know the opening did not identify Job’s loss as punishment.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions the friends’ explanation that God is punishing Job.

events.title: Job asks his friends for kindness
events.summary: Job describes pain beyond his strength. He compares his friends to streams that disappear when needed.
events.detail: Job compares his friends with water that disappears when travelers need it. The image concerns disappointed dependence, not merely harsh speech. Their promised help fails precisely when his need grows greatest.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job asks for kindness before a verdict. How could his friends answer that request?

events.title: Job addresses God in his pain
events.summary: Job describes sleepless nights and painful skin. He asks God to leave him alone.
events.detail: Job asks why God watches people so closely. Divine attention here feels burdensome rather than comforting. His appeal for rest challenges an easy equation between being seen and feeling safe.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job speaks directly to God about pain. What does he ask God to change?

events.title: Bildad blames wrongdoing
events.summary: Bildad suggests Job’s children died for their sins. He promises renewed success if Job is upright.
events.detail: Bildad explains the children’s deaths through their supposed sin. His tidy account gives Job another wound. Distinguish Bildad’s confidence from the book’s opening description of the household.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what goes wrong when friends explain pain through blame.

events.title: Job asks who could judge his case
events.summary: Job describes God’s power over mountains, stars, and seas. He seeks someone to hear both sides.
events.detail: Job pictures a dispute without an impartial judge between its parties. God’s power makes a fair hearing seem impossible. Legal language exposes his need for access, not simply a better defense.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job wants someone to hear both sides. What prevents him from feeling heard?

events.title: Job asks why his maker harms him
events.summary: Job recalls how God formed his body and gave him life. He asks why God now opposes him.
events.detail: Job recalls God carefully forming his body. He asks why its maker now seems to destroy it. The creation image gives his protest a personal claim on divine care.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job recalls the care that formed him. Why does his present pain make that memory difficult?

events.title: Zophar demands that Job change
events.summary: Zophar says Job deserves worse. He promises relief if Job removes wrongdoing from his home.
events.detail: Zophar claims Job deserves worse than his present suffering. His appeal to hidden wisdom prevents Job from challenging that claim. A speech about knowledge therefore ends by refusing to hear the sufferer.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions Zophar’s claim that Job’s pain comes from wrongdoing.

events.title: Job challenges his friends’ wisdom
events.summary: Job says he understands as much as his friends. He points to robbers who live safely.
events.detail: Job also knows the language of animals and divine power. That shared knowledge does not make his friends’ explanation true. He describes overturned rulers to question a simple connection between status and righteousness.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what Job knows about God while challenging his friends.

events.title: Job seeks a hearing with God
events.summary: Job accuses his friends of speaking falsely for God. He asks God to hear his case.
events.detail: Job calls his friends poor healers and challenges their defense of God. He wants to speak directly rather than accept their account. The scene asks whether religious loyalty excuses misleading claims about another person.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me follows the King James Bible’s reading about trusting God. How does that reading differ from the World English Bible here?

events.title: Job asks whether the dead live again
events.summary: Job compares short human life with a tree that can grow again. He asks God to remember him.
events.detail: A cut tree can send out new shoots. Job places that return beside human death and disappearance. His later wish for renewed life remains a question within this contrast.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects this question with resurrection through Jesus Christ. What does Job ask God to remember?

events.title: Eliphaz condemns Job’s words
events.summary: Eliphaz says Job’s own words prove guilt. He describes the fear and loss awaiting wicked people.
events.detail: Eliphaz now charges Job with undermining reverence itself. The dispute moves from Job’s circumstances to his right to speak. His account of wicked lives becomes accusation disguised as general instruction.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Eliphaz treats protest as proof of guilt. What happens when listeners make that assumption?

events.title: Job calls his friends poor comforters
events.summary: Job says he would strengthen them if their places were reversed. He asks for a witness in heaven.
events.detail: Job names his friends as failed comforters before seeking a witness above. Human listeners have not made his suffering understandable. His hope for testimony grows from the collapse of the present conversation.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how friends can strengthen someone instead of adding blame.

events.title: Job sees his hope nearing the grave
events.summary: Job describes broken plans and public shame. He asks where his hope can go.
events.detail: Job describes others calling darkness light while the grave approaches. Their assurances do not match the body before them. His questions about hope force readers to face that mismatch.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job’s plans have broken apart. What kind of help could reach him now?

events.title: Bildad describes the wicked person’s ruin
events.summary: Bildad describes traps, disease, lost children, and a forgotten name. He calls this the wicked person’s fate.
events.detail: Bildad describes traps, lost descendants, and destroyed homes. These images closely resemble Job’s losses without naming him. A speech presented as general wisdom therefore presses a personal accusation.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Bildad describes the loss of a name and children. How might Job hear those words?

events.title: Job asks for pity and a defender
events.summary: Job describes relatives, servants, and friends turning away. He declares that his Redeemer lives.
events.detail: Job asks the friends for pity before speaking of a defender. His damaged relationships make recognition as urgent as explanation. Read the hope for vindication beside his immediate request to stop the attack.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me reads Job’s Redeemer as Jesus Christ. A redeemer saves or defends someone. What help does Job hope for?

events.title: Zophar says wicked success ends quickly
events.summary: Zophar describes stolen wealth turning into suffering. He says wicked people cannot keep their success.
events.detail: The wicked person consumes riches and must give them back. This bodily image makes injustice seem certain to punish its owner. Job’s next speech challenges whether actual lives always follow that pattern.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Zophar links wickedness with brief success. What evidence would challenge his claim?

events.title: Job points to wicked people who prosper
events.summary: Job describes wicked people growing old with safe homes and thriving children. He challenges his friends’ answers.
events.detail: Job points to wicked people who live long and prosper. Their children and homes survive while his own did not. These examples test the friends’ explanation against events rather than merely another theory.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the contrast between wicked success and faithful suffering.

events.title: Eliphaz names sins he assumes Job committed
events.summary: Eliphaz accuses Job of withholding food, clothing, and help. He urges Job to return to God.
events.detail: Eliphaz now names specific offenses against poor people. The speech treats its explanation of suffering as evidence of those offenses. Compare these charges with Job’s later account of his public conduct.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Eliphaz’s accusation to ask how friends can offer better help.

events.title: Job searches for God’s court
events.summary: Job wants to present his case to God. He cannot find him, but insists he kept his commands.
events.detail: Job imagines presenting his case before God. He searches in every direction but cannot find that court. His confidence in his conduct exists beside fear of a power he cannot approach.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Job’s search with faith during unanswered questions.

events.title: Job describes the suffering of the poor
events.summary: Job describes stolen fields, hungry workers, and people without shelter. He asks why justice seems delayed.
events.detail: Job describes workers, hungry families, and people driven from shelter. Their injuries remain visible without swift public judgment. His protest now asks why a whole pattern of harm goes unanswered.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses other Church scripture to study suffering. Which examples show Job’s concern for people beyond himself?

events.title: Bildad questions human purity
events.summary: Bildad says God rules above and even the stars lack purity before him. He compares people to worms.
events.detail: Bildad answers with human smallness before God. This claim does not address the injured people Job just described. The shrinking response shows how general claims can avoid a concrete dispute.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Bildad speaks about human weakness. Does his answer address what Job asked?

events.title: Job describes power beyond human knowledge
events.summary: Job first asks how Bildad has helped him. He describes God’s power over sky, sea, and death.
events.detail: Job asks whom Bildad’s speech has strengthened. He then describes divine power in language equally grand. The contrast separates impressive claims about God from help that meets a sufferer’s need.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job asks how Bildad helped him. What separates an impressive speech from useful comfort?

events.title: Job holds to his innocence
events.summary: Job refuses to admit the friends are right about him. He then describes the fate of oppressors.
events.detail: Job will not confess guilt simply to end the dispute. His hold on integrity stands beside descriptions of wicked people’s ruin. Agreement about some judgments does not require accepting the friends’ charge against him.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job refuses a false confession. Why would admitting his friends are right matter?

events.title: Where can wisdom be found?
events.summary: A poem describes miners finding hidden metals. It asks where wisdom lies and says God knows its way.
events.detail: People can reach hidden metals beneath the earth. Yet the poem asks where wisdom can be found. The contrast separates technical success from understanding how life should be lived.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The poem separates treasure from wisdom. What can skill and wealth fail to teach?

events.title: Job remembers respect and service
events.summary: Job recalls public honor and his children nearby. He remembers helping widows and people in need.
events.detail: Job remembers helping people who lacked defenders. His former honor rests on these acts as well as wealth. Read this account against Eliphaz’s accusations about how he treated the poor.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job remembers helping people in need. How does that memory answer Eliphaz’s accusations?

events.title: Job describes shame and unanswered cries
events.summary: Job contrasts former respect with mockery and pain. He says his calls to God receive no answer.
events.detail: Job’s former respect becomes ridicule and isolation. His appeal to God receives no answer within the speech. The final change from music to mourning gives this reversal a sound.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Job’s neighbors add mockery to pain. What could they change without knowing why he suffers?

events.title: Job gives his final defense
events.summary: Job lists wrongs he says he avoided. He describes fairness toward servants, generosity, and welcome for strangers.
events.detail: Job asks for a fair weighing of his life. He then names concrete duties toward workers, poor people, and strangers. His claim concerns conduct, not only private feelings. The image of weighing makes impartial judgment visible. An ancient trade weight helps explain the image without identifying Job’s time or home.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me recalls Job’s repeated request for God to answer him.

events.title: Elihu begins after the others fall silent
events.summary: Elihu becomes angry with Job and his three friends. He says youth does not prevent understanding.
events.detail: Elihu explains why he waited before speaking. He then claims understanding does not belong to age alone. His entrance changes the speakers without yet providing readers an independent verdict on his claims.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu waited for older speakers. Does his anger help him listen?

events.title: Elihu says suffering can teach
events.summary: Elihu says God speaks through dreams and pain. He describes rescue through a messenger and renewed health.
events.detail: Elihu first stresses his shared human condition with Job. He then interprets dreams and pain as divine instruction. The move from equal listener to teacher helps explain the pressure within his appeal.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu says pain can teach. How could that idea help or hurt someone in distress?

events.title: Elihu defends God’s justice
events.summary: Elihu says God treats rich and poor without favor. He accuses Job of adding rebellion to sin.
events.detail: Elihu insists God cannot act wrongly. He uses that conviction to condemn Job’s words. The argument defends divine justice without answering the particular losses that produced Job’s protest.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu defends fairness while accusing Job. What evidence supports his charge?

events.title: Elihu challenges Job’s complaint
events.summary: Elihu says human choices affect other people. He claims pride prevents cries for help from being heard.
events.detail: Elihu links unanswered cries with pride and inadequate understanding. That claim shifts attention from oppression toward the petitioner. Read his explanation as Elihu’s judgment, not the book’s independent finding.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu links unanswered cries with pride. What would Job’s earlier words challenge?

events.title: Elihu describes correction and the storm
events.summary: Elihu says suffering opens people’s ears to instruction. He describes rain, clouds, and lightning.
events.detail: Elihu presents affliction as a means of opening ears. He also warns Job against choices that could worsen his condition. The speech combines an offer of meaning with pressure to accept it.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu promises good years after obedience. How does that promise compare with Job’s experience?

events.title: Elihu asks Job to consider God’s works
events.summary: Elihu describes thunder, snow, and changing weather. He asks whether Job understands their workings.
events.detail: Elihu asks Job to consider wonders beyond his control. Thunder and cloud imagery widen the scene beyond the dispute. The following divine speech comes from a whirlwind, continuing that change of scale.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Elihu asks about weather beyond human control. What changes when the next speaker is the Lord?

events.title: The Lord answers from the whirlwind
events.summary: The Lord questions Job about earth, sea, dawn, weather, stars, and animals.
events.detail: God’s questions begin with a world older than Job. They do not reveal the opening conversation that readers know. The reply changes the field of attention without giving a direct cause for the losses.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects the joyful sons of God with life before birth. What does God ask Job about creation?

events.title: The Lord describes wild animals
events.summary: The Lord asks about goats, wild donkeys, oxen, ostriches, horses, hawks, and eagles.
events.detail: The animals described here need not obey or benefit people. Their freedom and unusual habits matter within the speech. The world’s value therefore exceeds its usefulness to the person asking for an explanation.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how the creatures in God’s speech change the reader’s view.

events.title: Job falls silent and hears about behemoth
events.summary: Job places his hand over his mouth. The Lord questions his judgment and describes behemoth’s strength.
events.detail: God connects Job’s challenge with the ability to bring proud people low. The questions test more than skill in making an argument. The powerful creature that follows adds another limit to human control.
events.uncertainty: The poem names the Jordan. This marker does not locate Job’s home.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to consider God’s creations from different views.

events.title: The Lord describes Leviathan
events.summary: The Lord describes Leviathan’s scales, strength, and frightening breath. Human tools cannot subdue it.
events.detail: Questions about catching Leviathan turn into an account of its strength. The creature cannot become an ordinary servant or household possession. Its resistance makes human claims to command the wider world seem small.
events.uncertainty: Job’s home in Uz has no secure map location.

lds.text: The poem describes Leviathan beyond human control. What does that show about the limits of power?

events.title: Job answers and prays for his friends
events.summary: Job answers the Lord. The Lord rebukes the three friends. Job prays for them and receives renewed prosperity.
events.detail: God rejects the friends’ speech even though they defended divine justice. Job’s prayer for them then becomes part of the ending. Restoration does not supply a simple explanation for the earlier deaths. The book leaves a difference between renewed life and answered questions. Its final judgment warns against using certainty to explain another person’s pain.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects Job’s renewed life with hope after loss. What must the friends do after God corrects them?

guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: The reader knows what the friends do not

That difference shapes the long debate. Read confident advice against the book’s opening, not only the speaker’s certainty.

steps.title: A measure becomes an image of justice

The image of weighing makes impartial judgment visible. An ancient trade weight helps explain the image without identifying Job’s time or home.

steps.title: The final judgment changes how the speeches should be read
steps.text: God rejects the friends’ speech even though they defended divine justice. Job’s prayer for them then becomes part of the ending. Restoration does not supply a simple explanation for the earlier deaths. The book leaves a difference between renewed life and answered questions. Its final judgment warns against using certainty to explain another person’s pain.
